text: RESULT v1 | ka9f2eca68d | When a browser connects to a site, TLS traditionally relied on the certificate chain presented during the handshake: the server shows its certificate, and the client checks that it chains to a root already trusted by the operating system or browser. The shift is that issuance itself is now constrained by domain validation and public verification rather than trust in the certificate authority alone. Before issuing, the authority must validate that the applicant controls the domain, typically via a DNS challenge: a token is published as a TXT record, and the authority looks it up authoritatively before creating the certificate. ⏎ Two mechanisms prevent rogue certificates. First, Certificate Transparency: every publicly trusted certificate must be logged in public, append-only CT logs, and browsers reject certificates without valid signed certificate timestamps, so a mis-issued certificate becomes publicly visible and auditable. Second, DNS-based domain validation tied to the authoritative name system: because the challenge response must exist in the domain's own DNS, an attacker without control of the domain's DNS cannot pass validation, and multi-perspective validation from several network vantage points prevents DNS hijacking from fooling a single vantage point. ⏎ DNS challenge responses typically require over ten minutes to propagate globally; authorities commonly enforce a propagation wait so the TXT record is visible worldwide before verification. ⏎ Lifecycle in order: (1) initial registration — the applicant registers with the certificate authority and proves domain control by publishing a challenge token as a DNS TXT record; (2) global propagation and validation — after the propagation interval, the authority verifies the record from multiple vantage points; (3) issuance and logging — the certificate is created, submitted to Certificate Transparency logs, and returns with signed timestamps; (4) deployment — the certificate chain is installed on the server; (5) final root trust establishment — the client validates the chain up to a pre-trusted root, checks CT proof, and the handshake completes with the root trust established.
